answer.answer:
Adopting a robotic process means changing the delivery model itself: the contract form, the business model and the work culture around the job, and alongside that moving fabrication off-site, standardising the components the robot handles, and training the workforce. Of the requirements sitting upstream of robotic assembly, only one is actually a machine; the rest are organisational or process changes, which is where the real adoption effort goes. The requirements are also very unequal in the record: training and standardisation are drawn on by most of the coded cases, while the delivery-model change is asserted in the literature and exhibited by only 2 of the 50, and an all-weather mobile factory by none. Early contractor involvement and vertical integration are the two concrete levers for pulling production knowledge into design.

**The delivery-model requirement itself**

Robotic assembly (PR4) depends on Delivery/business model/work culture (RI12): robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [1] (DEP61), backed by peer-reviewed evidence. In the relation `dependsOn`, RI12 is the requirement, so the delivery and business-model change comes first in practice. 16 of the 50 coded cases draw on RI12 [2], but DEP61 is carried by only 2 of the 50 coded cases [2], meaning only two cases draw on both ends. The same requirement recurs at scale: AT8 "Industrialised" dependsOn RI12, because adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models (DEP81), carried by 13 of the 50 [2]. RI12 carries 2 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges, all of them listed [2], so these two are the whole of its dependency structure in the graph.

**What else has to change upstream of robotic assembly**

PR4 carries 4 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges [2], and the requirement side is uneven:

- AT7 "Highly standardised" enablesCapability PR4, since Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components (DEP88), carried by 10 of the 50 [2]; 25 of the 50 cases draw on AT7 [2].
- PR4 hasPrecondition PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", because automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials (DEP55), carried by 4 of the 50 [2]; 20 cases draw on PR2 [2].
- PR12 "Path-planning" enablesCapability PR4 as a precondition for robotic assembly (DEP23), carried by 2 of the 50 [2]; 26 cases draw on PR12 [2].
- PR4 dependsOn RE2 "Robotic arm" (DEP24), carried by 12 of the 50 [2]; 22 cases draw on RE2 [2]. This is the one Resource, the one piece of hardware, among the requirements.
- CO12 "Mobile factory" enablesCapability PR4 (DEP42) is carried by 0 of the 50 coded cases [2], and only 1 of the 50 draws on CO12 [2]: cited in the literature, carried by none of the 50.

**Workforce and safety**

Human-robot interaction (CO6) dependsOn RI6 "Require workforce training", since the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce (DEP34), carried by 27 of the 50 [2], and the automated production workflow (AR9) likewise dependsOn RI6 (DEP100), carried by 38 of the 50 [2]; 44 of the 50 cases draw on RI6 [2]. This is by far the best-carried change in the set. CO6 also dependsOn RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern", on compliance with robot safety standards (DEP45), carried by 2 of the 50 [2], and CO6 mitigates RI20 "Work safety concern" through power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation (DEP57), carried by 4 of the 50 [2]: only one cited path in this material runs to site safety, and the context does not establish that it is the only one in the record.

**Procurement levers**

Early contractor involvement (CO11) enablesCapability PR2 "Prefabrication/off-site", because integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase and a delivery method that does so should be selected (DEP22), carried by 13 of the 50 [2]; CO11 also enablesCapability PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process" (DEP77), carried by 11 of the 50 [2], and enablesCapability AT12 "Integrated design-DFAB process" (DEP65), carried by 10 [2]. 14 of the 50 draw on CO11 [2]. On the organisational side, AT12 hasPrecondition CO10 "Vertical integration", on the argument that technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm (DEP35), carried by 14 of the 50 [2]; 25 of the 50 draw on CO10 [2].

**Deployed record**

Two deployed assembly processes are in front of me. census_RXH4-1 performs assembly and concrete work on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9, adopted to address cost and labor [3]; it is manufactured by Firm_166 and uses concrete [4]. census_RXH7-2 performs assembly and tiling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, at technology readiness level 9, adopted to address quality, safety, labor and market [5], manufactured by Firm_125 and recorded as a census record of process RP29 [4]. That market driver is the closest the deployed record here comes to a business-model motive. Note, though, that the context links neither case to RI12 or to any other enabler, so I cannot say these cases exhibit the delivery-model change; the evidence for it is the dependency record and its 2 carrying cases.

One widening to flag: retrieval read "robotic process" broadly, but the delivery-model dependency attaches specifically to robotic assembly (PR4) and to industrialised scale (AT8). RE10 "Gantry-type robotic system", drawn on by 5 of the 50, carries no dependency edges [2], and PR15 "Robotic pickup/selection", drawn on by 19, carries none either [2], so nothing in front of me ties delivery change to those forms.
